chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Hajjal, from Thal'abah ibn Maymun, from Sa'id ibn Amr al-Ju'fi, who said:

I went out to Mecca while I was among the people in the most difficult financial condition, so I complained to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). When I left his presence, I found a bag at his door containing seven hundred dinars. I returned to him immediately and informed him. He said: 'O Sa'id, fear Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and present it among the gatherings,' and I hoped that he would allow me to keep it.

So I went out gloomy, and I came to Mina and secluded myself from the people, searching until I reached the standing place (Mawqif). I lodged in a room away from the people. Then I said, 'Who recognizes the bag?' The first voice I heard was from a man above me saying, 'I am the owner of the bag.' I said to myself, 'You, so be it.' I asked, 'What is the mark of the bag?' He informed me of its mark, so I handed it over to him.

He said: So he went aside and counted them, and the dinars were in their original state. Then he counted seventy dinars from them and said, 'Take these; they are permissible, better than seven hundred prohibited ones.' So I took them. Then I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and informed him of how I secluded myself and what I did. He said: 'Indeed, when you complained to me, we ordered thirty dinars for you. O Maid, bring them!' So I took them, and I was among my people in the best financial condition.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on found property and the story of the bag of dinars in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narrative from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Shia jurisprudence of *al-mal al-mafqud* (found property), highlighting the tension between public proclamation (*ta'rif*) and the virtue of private retention to avoid ostentation. The Imam’s revelation of the pre-ordained thirty dinars underscores the concept of divine providence (*tawfiq*) and the spiritual merit of sincerity (*ikhlas*) over material gain, a key theme in Twelver hadith literature regarding ethical conduct in commerce and charity.
